# Stashing Changes

## A pull that won't go through

Picture this: you're in the middle of editing a file — a half-finished thought you're [not ready to commit]{.uwred} — when you remember you should pull a teammate's latest work first.

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

You run `git pull`, and Git [refuses]{.uwred}. Your uncommitted edits are in the way: the pull would overwrite them, so Git stops to protect your work.

<div class="gap-md"></div>

[`git stash`]{.uwred} is the way out. It sets your unfinished changes aside, hands you a clean working tree, and lets you bring them back when you're ready.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The setup: you're mid-edit

Back in your main copy of the repo, you start tweaking `brats.txt` — jotting how many brats to buy per person:

```bash
cd ~/github/gameday-menu
nano brats.txt
```

```
Buy 3 brats per person
```

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

You haven't committed — this is a work in progress:

```bash
git status
```

```
On branch main
Changes not staged for commit:
  (use "git add <file>..." to update what will be committed)
	modified:   brats.txt
```


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Meanwhile, GitHub has moved on

While you were typing, [Sam]{.uwred} pushed an update to `brats.txt` up to GitHub (a different line — the brand to buy).

<div class="gap-md"></div>

So the version on GitHub is now ahead of yours, and it touches the [same file]{.uwred} you're editing. That's exactly the situation where a plain pull gets stuck.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The pull is blocked

You try to grab Sam's change:

```bash
git pull
```

```
error: Your local changes to the following files would be overwritten by merge:
	brats.txt
Please commit your changes or stash them before you merge.
Aborting
```

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

Git offers two ways forward: [commit]{.uwred} your changes, or [stash]{.uwred} them. A half-finished thought isn't worth a commit yet — so you stash.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Set it aside: `git stash`

Tuck your uncommitted changes away:

```bash
git stash
```

```
Saved working directory and index state WIP on main: 9f8e7d6 Merge: offer both ice cream flavors
```

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

Your edits are safely parked, and the working tree is back to the last commit — [clean]{.uwred}:

```bash
git status
```

```
On branch main
nothing to commit, working tree clean
```

::: {.footer}
Give a stash a label so you remember what it holds: `git stash push -m "wip: brat quantities"`.
:::


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## See what's parked: `git stash list`

Your set-aside work lives in a stack you can inspect any time:

```bash
git stash list
```

```
stash@{0}: WIP on main: 9f8e7d6 Merge: offer both ice cream flavors
```

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

[`stash@{0}`]{.uwred} is the most recent entry. For now there's just one — which is how you want to keep it.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Now the pull succeeds

With a clean tree, Git can bring Sam's change down without stepping on anything:

```bash
git pull
```

```
Updating 9f8e7d6..e4f5a6b
Fast-forward
 brats.txt | 1 +
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
```

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

Your local `brats.txt` now has Sam's update — but your own half-finished edit is still waiting in the stash.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Bring it back: `git stash pop`

Reapply your parked changes on top of the freshly pulled file:

```bash
git stash pop
```

```
Auto-merging brats.txt
On branch main
Changes not staged for commit:
	modified:   brats.txt

Dropped refs/stash@{0} (f0a1b2c3d4e5f6a7b8c9d0e1f2a3b4c5d6e7f8a9)
```

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

Your work-in-progress is back on top of Sam's update, and the stash entry is [gone]{.uwred}. Finish your thought, then `git add` and `git commit` as usual.

::: {.footer}
If your edits and the pulled change touched the same line, `pop` reports a conflict — resolve it exactly as in the Conflicts unit.
:::


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## A few things to know

- A stash is [local only]{.uwred} — it never travels to GitHub. It's for short-term juggling, not long-term storage.
- [`git stash pop`]{.uwred} reapplies your work and removes the entry; [`git stash apply`]{.uwred} reapplies it but leaves the entry in the list.
- Plain `git stash` leaves brand-new [untracked]{.uwred} files behind. Add `-u` (`git stash -u`) to sweep those in too.

<div class="gap-md"></div>

Good habit: pop a stash [soon]{.uwred}. A pile of forgotten stashes is hard to untangle later.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Your turn

::: {.callout-wide}
::: {.callout-important}
# Try it
Stash, sync, and restore:

1. Edit `cheese_curds.txt` but [don't]{.uwred} commit
2. Run `git stash`, then confirm `git status` is clean
3. `git pull` to sync with GitHub
4. `git stash pop` to bring your edit back, then finish and commit it
:::
:::


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Where we are

Stashing lets you step away from unfinished work without committing it:

- [`git stash`]{.uwred} parks your uncommitted changes and cleans the working tree
- [`git stash pop`]{.uwred} brings them back; [`git stash list`]{.uwred} shows what's parked
- It's the cleanest way to let a blocked [`git pull`]{.uwred} go through

<div class="gap-md"></div>
